source.title: Before Retrieval Begins: Safety and Tool-Use Decisions in LLM Agents
source.authors: Aditya Nawal; Manit Baser; M. Gurusamy

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a text-refusal direction as an intervention to examine tool admission, but does not test whether the claim’s refusal direction causes refusal or induces refusals of harmless requests.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results on refusal–tool-call divergence and on how refusal-related and requested-operation directions affect tool admission. Those outcomes are about tool admission, not the refusal behaviors named by V1–V8; the related results are recorded with versions ["none"]. Its citations to prior work on refusal directions are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-of-means and projection-removal method of Arditi et al. as a tool. Its outcome is tool admission (whether a well-formed tool call is emitted), not text refusal. Its text-refusal direction contrasts refusal and compliant responses, not harmful and harmless instructions. It is never ablated or added to measure refusal or other abilities. Steering it is scored only on tool calls, a related but different construct, so no V1–V8 version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. Fuller version: harmful tool admission is shaped mostly by the requested-operation component (19 pp vs 8 pp for topic). A direction from that contrast influences held-out admission in four of seven models, without being operation-specific. Written refusal is only partially coupled to admission: it accompanies 33.6% of admitted harmful calls, and steering effects are heterogeneous. Single-seed refusal fine-tuning cut admission in three models that kept benign tool use. The authors conclude admission should be evaluated and supervised directly.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates requested-operation and text-refusal directions and tests tool admission, rather than testing the original harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction against refusal outcomes. It does not test addition-induced refusals of harmless requests.
record.method_sensitivity: The direction-removal effect varies by model and between operation-present and operation-neutralized requests. Text-refusal steering effects vary substantially across models and dose/control conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Genuine written refusals accompany 33.6% of admitted harmful tool calls, ranging from 0% (Mistral-7B) to 46.6% (Mistral-Nemo).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Written refusal and harmful tool admission can diverge within one turn.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering a text-refusal direction at the tool-decision token shifts tool admission in four models with valid controls. Shifts range from −71.4 to +11.9 pp, in both directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A text-refusal direction influences tool admission in a model-dependent and sign-inconsistent way.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out removal of a requested-operation difference-of-means direction raises admission by 2.0–9.5 pp in four of seven models. It sometimes also moves operation-neutralized requests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A direction from the requested-operation contrast can influence tool admission, but it is not specific to harmful-operation semantics.

fits_no_version.finding: The text-refusal direction is anti-aligned with the admission-outcome direction in all models (Fig. 4). Plain-text refusal fine-tuning lowers harmful admission by 19.6–61.5 pp in three models that keep benign calling (Table 18). Other runs collapse benign use or fail.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-refusal representations and training partially transfer to the tool-call decision.

record.problems: The text-refusal steering uses exploratory per-model doses and has saturated or floor controls for some models. The refusal fine-tuning pilot uses one recipe and one seed per model; several runs do not isolate refusal transfer because benign tool use collapses or generation fails. The intervention results concern tool admission, not the claim’s refusal outcome.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows omitted. The paper also reports factorial request-component contrasts, broad harm rates, prompt defenses, monitoring results, and fine-tuning outcomes; these concern tool admission or tool-use safety rather than the specified refusal-direction versions.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless direction measured on refusal; no capability check. Steering a refusal-vs-compliance direction is scored only on tool admission.
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training against ablation.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction refusal structure.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer of a refusal direction.
Refusal fine-tuning is measured on tool admission only. It does not test whether training decides that a removable refusal direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Arditi et al. for the projection-removal method and applies it to non-refusal directions and a non-refusal outcome. The fine-tuning and geometry results are not row-recorded. They concern tool admission and bear on no version, so they appear under fits_no_version rather than missing.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and measure refusal, add that direction and measure refusals of harmless requests, or assess preservation of other abilities under that intervention.
No weight-edit or abliteration evaluation of refusal.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not test whether refusal is represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test of the refusal direction.
Fine-tunes on plain-text refusals and measures tool admission, but does not test whether training choices determine the existence of a removable refusal direction.
